study.title: Evolution of the experience with the semiconstrained distal radioulnar joint arthroplasty: A single center review of medium-term outcomes and complications
study.journal: Journal of hand surgery global online

cover.headline: When wrist joints wear out, **a metal implant can reduce pain and keep motion stable** for years.

slides.title: The distal radioulnar joint connects your forearm bones at the wrist, and when it fails, turning your palm hurts.
slides.body:
Injury, arthritis, and other conditions can destroy this joint. Surgeons have increasingly turned to a semiconstrained implant called the Aptis to replace it, but medium-term data on how well it works—and what goes wrong—has been limited.

This team in a single center tracked 36 implants in 34 patients over an average of 4.4 years to see how pain, motion, and weight-bearing ability evolved, and how often revision surgery was needed.

slides.title: Pain dropped significantly after surgery, and active range of motion plus weight-bearing ability stayed stable over time.
slides.body:
In the 15 patients with complete data and a surviving implant, the before-and-after comparison showed meaningful pain relief. No infections occurred. The implant itself survived in 91% of cases at a mean follow-up of 53 months.

But 27% of patients needed revision surgery for complications. The authors stress that extremely precise surgical technique is mandatory—small errors in placement or tension can lead to problems that require a second operation.

caveats: This study found a pattern, not a cause—something else could explain the link between the implant and the outcomes.
Sample size was 34 patients. Worth replicating in a larger group before anyone changes practice.

cta.headline: Science worth sharing lives here
cta.sub: Follow for the studies that actually move the conversation forward.

caption:
A specialized wrist implant is linked to lasting pain relief and stable function in people whose distal radioulnar joint has failed. Thirty-four patients received the Aptis semiconstrained implant between 2010 and 2021, and surgeons tracked pain, range of motion, and weight bearing over an average of 4.4 years. Pain levels dropped significantly, and motion stayed consistent. The implant survived in 91% of cases at 53 months, but more than a quarter of patients needed revision surgery—underscoring how technically demanding the procedure is. Published in Journal of Hand Surgery Global Online. The study was observational and relatively small. One limitation: only 15 patients had complete data for the before-and-after comparison. Full study: doi.org/10.1016/j.jhsg.2026.101117
